**Fighting the borrow checker instead of learning from it.**

The most common anti-pattern in Rust is reaching for **`Arc<Mutex<T>>`** (or `Rc<RefCell<T>>` on the single-threaded side) every time the compiler complains about borrows. It compiles, but it's a code smell — you're using runtime checks to work around a problem the type system is trying to help you solve statically.

Same goes for slapping **`.clone()`** on everything or using `.unwrap()` / `.expect("")` liberally instead of handling errors properly. These all have one thing in common: they paper over the compiler's hints rather than addressing the root cause.

The better approach: when the borrow checker rejects your code, it's usually telling you your data flow is tangled. Restructure — split functions, narrow scopes, return owned values instead of mutating in place. It takes more mental effort upfront, but the result is code that's genuinely safer and faster than its `Arc<Mutex<T>>` equivalent.
